transcript: Okay, Sarah Snook getting a Tony Award is probably one of the more certain things in the world right now. She's playing over two dozen characters in a one-woman stage adaptation of The Picture of Dorian Gray and she is simply astonishing. I love the original novel and I wasn't sure how well it would translate to the stage, but this version written and directed by Kip Williams is like nothing you would expect. I don't wanna give it all away, but the use of technology here is crazy. There's obviously live acting, but there's also live streaming, live superimposing, even some live photoshopping. It's a very inventive and meta hybrid between a theater piece and a film where you can see the pictures being created on the screens while observing the stagework that’s simultaneously going on behind the scenes. In some ways, the whole thing is a bit gimmicky, but that doesn't make it bad. Actually, I think what impressed me the most about Sarah's performance was how well she's able to access emotions within such a chaotic-looking but surely precise set of choreographed traffic patterns involving cameras, set pieces, and screens. She doesn't have scene partners. She just has cameras, screens, and sometimes other versions of herself on the screens. But she is locked in carrying a two-hour performance which must be exhausting to do eight times a week. The stamina and the focus to maintain the pace of this show is wild, and not just for Sarah, but for the extensively involved crew on and off stage as well. All that's to say, I would absolutely recommend this, but a word of wisdom is to not sit too close. The production relies heavily on screens, and with a bit of distance, I think you'll get a lot more out of it by being able to see multiple screens at once. And at more of a comfortable angle, your neck will thank you afterwards. With that, another playbill for my collection.
